title: Acintyabhedābheda
description: The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava doctrine of acintyabhedābheda (inconceivable simultaneous oneness and difference), associated with Jīva Gosvāmī, stating that the relationship between Kṛṣṇa and his potencies is beyond logical categorization; its epistemological and theological implications are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Advaita Adhyāsa
description: In Advaita Vedānta, adhyāsa (superimposition) is the erroneous attribution of the qualities of the non-self (anatman) to the self (ātman); its definition, types (svarūpa and samsarga), and role in bondage are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Advaita Ajāti-vāda
description: The Advaita doctrine of ajāti-vāda (non-origination), associated with Gauḍapāda, asserting that the world of birth and death never truly originates and that Brahman alone is real; its arguments and relation to Māṇḍūkya Kārikā are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Advaita Avidyā
description: In Advaita Vedānta, avidyā (nescience) is the beginningless ignorance that veils Brahman and projects the world of multiplicity; its nature as neither real nor unreal (anirvacanīya), its locus, and its removal through brahma-jñāna are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Āgamic Tradition
description: The Āgamic (Tantric) tradition: the Śaiva Āgamas (28 principal texts), Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātras and Vaikhānasas, Śākta Tantras; their structure (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā), their role in temple ritual, iconography, and initiation (dīkṣā); their distinction from Vedic orthopraxy and their integration into Smārta tradition are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Alaṅkāra Śāstra
description: The Sanskrit poetics tradition analyzing figures of speech (alaṅkāras), poetic merits (guṇas), and aesthetic defects (doṣas); its major texts and theorists are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Anubandha Catuṣṭaya
description: The four preliminary factors traditionally stated at the beginning of a Vedānta work: adhikārin (qualified student), viṣaya (subject), prayojana (purpose), and sambandha (relationship).

title: Āpaddharma
description: The Dharmaśāstra concept of āpaddharma (dharma in times of distress/emergency): the relaxation of normal rules for survival, the hierarchy of permissible actions, and the principle that normal dharma resumes when the emergency passes; its textual basis in Manusmṛti and other Smṛtis is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Apparatus Criticus
description: The critical apparatus in a scholarly edition recording variant readings, editorial decisions, and conjectures; its formats (positive, negative, hybrid) are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Arjuna
description: The third Pāṇḍava, renowned archer and recipient of the Bhagavad Gītā; traditional narratives and textual portrayals are represented without historical conflation.

title: Artha
description: One of the four puruṣārthas, referring to material prosperity, power, and security; its pursuit is contextualized by dharma in textual traditions.

title: Āśrama Dharma
description: The four āśramas (stages of life) in Dharmaśāstra: brahmacarya (student), gṛhastha (householder), vānaprastha (forest-dweller), and saṃnyāsa (renunciant); their duties (dharma), transitions (saṃskāras), and the ideal progression toward mokṣa are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Āśrama
description: The four-stage model of life—brahmacarya, gṛhastha, vānaprastha, saṃnyāsa—whose applicability and interpretation vary across texts and historical periods.

title: Atharvaveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Atharvaveda: Śaunaka (the principal surviving recension) and Paippalāda (partially preserved in Kashmir and Orissa); their textual differences and the Atharvaveda's unique character among the four Vedas are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Ātman
description: A term for the self or innermost principle whose nature and relationship to Brahman constitute a central question in Upaniṣadic and Vedāntic thought.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapters
description: The eighteen adhyāyas (chapters) of the Bhagavad Gītā, their thematic progression from viṣāda-yoga to mokṣa-sannyāsa-yoga, and their philosophical themes (karma-yoga, jñāna-yoga, bhakti-yoga) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Bhagavad Gītā Philosophy
description: The philosophical teachings of the Bhagavad Gītā: the synthesis of karma-yoga (selfless action), jñāna-yoga (knowledge), and bhakti-yoga (devotion); the nature of the self (ātman), the supreme (puruṣottama), the three guṇas, and the concept of svadharma; its influence on later Vedānta schools are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Bhakti Movement
description: The Bhakti movement (7th–17th centuries): the devotional renaissance across India emphasizing personal devotion (bhakti) to a chosen deity (iṣṭa-devatā) over ritual orthodoxy; its poet-saints (Āḻvārs, Nāyanārs, Vārkarīs, Haridāsas, Rāmānanda, Kabīr, Tulsīdās, Mīrābāī, Sūrdās, Caitanya); its vernacular literature, social egalitarianism, and lasting impact on Hindu practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Bhakti
description: Devotional orientation or practice whose objects, methods, and theological frameworks vary widely across texts, traditions, and historical periods.

title: Bharatanatyam Repertoire
description: The traditional Bharatanatyam performance repertoire (mārgam): alarippu (invocation), jatisvaram (pure dance), śabdam (lyric dance), varṇam (centerpiece), padam (abhinaya), tillāṇa (finale), and ślokam/maṅgalam (conclusion); the role of nattuvanār, the mridangam, violin, and flute accompaniment are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Bhedābheda Avibhāga-bheda
description: The Bhedābheda doctrine of avibhāga-bheda (difference-in-non-difference), asserting that the whole and its parts are simultaneously different and non-different (like fire and its sparks); its variants in Bhāskara, Yādavaprakāśa, and Nimbārka are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Bhedābheda
description: The "difference and non-difference" doctrine, positing that the individual self and Brahman are simultaneously distinct and non-distinct; foundational for Viśiṣṭādvaita and other schools.

title: Bhīṣma
description: The grandsire of the Kuru dynasty, known for his vow of celibacy and role in the Mahābhārata; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Brahman
description: The ultimate reality or ground of being in Vedāntic traditions, described through both negation (neti neti) and positive affirmation depending on the school.

title: Carnatic Rāga System
description: The Carnatic rāga system: the 72 melakartā (parent) rāgas organized in the kaṭapayādi formula, their janya (derived) rāgas; the rāga structure (ārohaṇa/avarohaṇa), the gamaka (ornamentation), and the role of rāga in conveying rasa (emotion) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Camakam
description: The Camakam, the second part of the Śrī Rudram (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.7), listing the desired boons for the yajamāna; its repetitive structure (ca me) and ritual use alongside the Namakam are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Chandas
description: The Vedāṅga of metre and prosody, governing the rhythmic structure of Vedic and classical Sanskrit verse.

title: Codicology
description: The study of manuscripts as physical objects: materials, structure, binding, layout, and production; its methods and descriptive standards are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Collation
description: The systematic comparison of manuscript witnesses to record variant readings; its methods (manual, mechanical, digital) and output formats are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Colophon
description: The concluding note in a manuscript recording scribe, date, place, patron, or other production details; its formulaic variations across traditions are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Critical Edition
description: The scholarly reconstruction of a text from multiple manuscript witnesses, applying textual criticism to establish the most probable original reading; its methods and principles are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Dāna Types
description: The classification of dāna (gift) in Dharmaśāstra: nitya (daily), naimittika (occasional), kāmya (desire-motivated), and vimukti (liberation-oriented); the qualified recipients (supātra), objects, and occasions for giving are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Dāna
description: The practice of giving or gift-giving, regulated in Dharmaśāstra by donor, recipient, gift-type, and occasion; a key householder duty.

title: Darśana
description: Darśana (auspicious sight): the act of beholding a deity, guru, or sacred object in Hindu practice; its theological significance as a two-way exchange of grace (the deity sees the devotee, the devotee sees the deity); its role in temple worship, pilgrimage (tīrtha-yātrā), and guru-seva are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Dharma
description: A foundational concept whose meanings include duty, law, virtue, and the inherent nature of things; its specific sense depends on textual and situational context.

title: Dharmasūtra
description: The earliest genre of Dharma literature, composed in sūtra style and associated with Vedic schools; distinct from the later metrical Smṛtis.

title: Digital Humanities
description: The interdisciplinary field applying computational methods to humanities research; its Indian studies projects, text analysis, and infrastructure are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Digitization
description: The process of creating digital surrogates of manuscripts (imaging, metadata, OCR/HTR); its standards (FADGI, Metamorfoze), workflows, and access models are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Draupadī
description: The wife of the five Pāṇḍavas, central to the Mahābhārata narrative; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Durgā Forms
description: The forms of Durgā: the nine Navadurgās (Śailaputrī, Brahmacāriṇī, Chandraghaṇṭā, Kūṣmāṇḍā, Skandamātā, Kātyāyanī, Kālarātrī, Mahāgaurī, Siddhidātrī); the ten Mahāvidyās; the warrior Caṇḍikā and the mother Ambikā; their iconography, the Devī Māhātmya narrative, and the Navarātri festival are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Durgā
description: A form of the Goddess with major textual, ritual, and festival presence; represented here without imposing a single theological interpretation across Śākta traditions.

title: Duryodhana
description: The eldest Kaurava and primary antagonist of the Mahābhārata war; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Dvaita Pañca-bheda
description: The Dvaita Vedānta doctrine of five eternal differences (pañca-bheda): between Brahman (Viṣṇu) and jīva, between Brahman and jagat, between jīva and jīva, between jīva and jagat, and between jagat and jagat; their epistemic and ontological status are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Dvaita Sākṣi-bhāva
description: In Dvaita Vedānta, the sākṣi-bhāva (witness-consciousness) of the jīva is its capacity to witness its own mental states while remaining distinct from them; its role in self-knowledge and liberation is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Emendation
description: An editorial correction proposed where all manuscript witnesses appear corrupt; its justification, notation, and scholarly conventions are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Epigraphy
description: The study of inscriptions on durable materials (stone, metal, copper plates) for historical, linguistic, and cultural reconstruction; its methods and Indian corpora are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Folio
description: A single leaf of a manuscript (two pages: recto and verso); its numbering, structure, and descriptive conventions are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Gāndhārī
description: The wife of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and mother of the Kauravas, known for her voluntary blindness; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Gaṇeśa Forms
description: The forms of Gaṇeśa: Bāl Gaṇeśa, Taruṇa Gaṇeśa, Bhakti Gaṇeśa, Vīra Gaṇeśa, Śakti Gaṇeśa, Dvija Gaṇeśa, Siddhi Gaṇeśa, Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇeśa, Vighna Gaṇeśa, Kṣipra Gaṇeśa, Heramba Gaṇeśa, and Lakṣmī Gaṇeśa; their iconographic variations and the thirty-two forms tradition are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gāyatrī Mantra
description: The Gāyatrī Mantra (Ṛgveda 3.62.10), addressed to Savitṛ, is the most revered Vedic mantra; its metre (gāyatrī), traditional initiation (upadeśa), and role in sandhyāvandana are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gāyatrī
description: A celebrated Vedic metre and the hymn composed in it (Ṛgveda 3.62.10); also personified as a deity in later traditions.

title: Gītā Bhakti-yoga
description: The Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of bhakti-yoga (the yoga of devotion): the qualities of the devotee (bhakta), the nature of divine love, and the supremacy of bhakti as the path to liberation; its exposition across chapters 7–12 and 18 is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gītā Dhyāna
description: The traditional meditative verses recited before studying the Bhagavad Gītā, invoking the text and its lineage; represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Gītā Jñāna-yoga
description: The Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of jñāna-yoga (the yoga of knowledge): the distinction between kṣetra (field) and kṣetrajña (knower of the field), the nature of the self (ātman), and the realization of brahman; its exposition across chapters 13–18 is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gītā Karma-yoga
description: The Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of karma-yoga (the yoga of selfless action): niṣkāma-karma (action without attachment to fruits), svadharma (one's own duty), and the synthesis of action and knowledge; its exposition across chapters 2–5 is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gītā Māhātmya
description: The traditional texts extolling the greatness of the Bhagavad Gītā, found in various Purāṇas; represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Guru-Śiṣya Paramparā
description: The guru-śiṣya paramparā (teacher-disciple lineage): the oral transmission of knowledge (vidyā) from guru to śiṣya across generations; its role in Vedic, Vedānta, Yoga, Tantra, and artistic traditions; the concepts of dīkṣā (initiation), śraddhā (faith), and the guru as the embodiment of the teaching; its continuity in contemporary traditions are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Hanumān Forms
description: The forms of Hanumān (Añjanīputra, Māruti, Vāyusuta): the five-faced (pañcamukha) Hanumān, the eleven Rudra manifestations, the vīra (heroic) and dāsya (servitude) aspects; his iconography ( gadā, mountain, saṅjīvanī), his role in Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, and his worship across India are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Hanumān
description: A figure of the Rāmāyaṇa tradition whose devotional significance extends across Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva contexts; represented here without collapsing tradition-specific narratives.

title: Hare Kṛṣṇa Mahāmantra
description: The sixteen-word Vaiṣṇava mahāmantra (Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare / Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare), its centrality in Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava practice, and its source in the Kali-santaraṇa Upaniṣad are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Hindustani Gharānā
description: The Hindustani gharanā (lineage/school) system: the major vocal gharanās (Gwalior, Agra, Jaipur-Atrauli, Kirana, Patiala, Bhendi Bazaar, Indore, Mewati, Rampur-Sahaswan) and instrumental gharanās (Imdadkhani/Etawah sitar, Maihar sarod, etc.); the guru-śiṣya paramparā, distinctive gayaki/baaj (style), and their historical development are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Īśvara
description: A term for the Supreme Lord or personal God, whose ontological status and attributes are interpreted differently across Vedānta schools and Yoga philosophy.

title: Itihāsa Saṃskāra
description: The cultural impact of the Itihāsas (Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa) on Indian civilization: their role in shaping values, performing arts (Kathakali, Yakṣagāṇa, Rāmalīlā), temple iconography, regional languages, and the transmission of dharma across generations; their oral and textual transmission are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Jaiminīya Śākhā
description: The Jaiminīya Śākhā (also Talavakāra Śākhā) is a recension of the Sāmaveda, prevalent in South India; its texts include the Jaiminīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka, and Upaniṣad; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Japa Mālā
description: The japa-mālā (prayer beads) used for counting mantra repetitions: the standard 108 beads, the meru (guru bead), materials (rudrākṣa, tulasī, sphatika, etc.), and the rules for its use in japa practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Jīvanmukti
description: Liberation while living, a key concept in Advaita Vedānta and other traditions; its nature and attainability are interpreted differently across schools.

title: Jñāna
description: A term for knowledge, particularly liberating knowledge, whose content and means of attainment differ across philosophical schools and practice traditions.

title: Jyotiṣa
description: The Vedāṅga of astronomy and calendrical science, used for determining ritual times and celestial observations.

title: Kalpa
description: The Vedāṅga of ritual procedure, comprising Śrauta, Gṛhya, and Dharma sūtras that prescribe sacrificial and domestic rites.

title: Kāma
description: One of the four puruṣārthas, referring to desire, pleasure, and aesthetic enjoyment; its legitimate pursuit is bounded by dharma in textual traditions.

title: Kāṇva Śākhā
description: The Kāṇva Śākhā is a principal recension of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda; its texts include the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Kāṇva recension), Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Kāṇva), and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Kāṇva); represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kāpiṣṭhala Śākhā
description: The Kāpiṣṭhala Śākhā is a recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, closely related to the Kaṭha Śākhā; its texts are partially preserved; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Karma
description: A principle of action and consequence whose scope and mechanics are interpreted differently across philosophical traditions and textual layers.

title: Karṇa
description: A central figure of the Mahābhārata, known for his generosity and tragic role; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Kaṭha Śākhā
description: The Kaṭha Śākhā is a recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; its texts include the Kaṭha Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka, and the Kaṭha Upaniṣad; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kathakali Vesham
description: The Kathakali vesham (makeup/costume) classification: paccā (green, noble/heroic), kaṭṭi (knife, anti-heroic), kari (black, demonic), teṭṭa (beard, ascetic), minukku (polished, female/sage); the symbolic colors, the chutti (white ridge), and the elaborate headgear (kireetam) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kauthuma Śākhā
description: The Kauthuma Śākhā is the principal surviving recension of the Sāmaveda; its texts include the Sāmaveda Saṃhitā, Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa, Chāndogya Upaniṣad, and Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kṛṣṇa Forms
description: The forms of Kṛṣṇa: the infant Bāla Gopāla, the cowherd Gopīnātha, the flute-player Veṇugopāla, the cow-lifter Govardhana-dhārī, the charioteer Pārtha-sārathi, the universal form Viśvarūpa, and the supreme Parabrahman; their iconography, associated texts (Bhāgavata, Gītā, Harivaṃśa), and regional worship (Vṛndāvana, Dvārakā, Nāthadvāra) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kṛṣṇa
description: A central figure of the Mahābhārata and Bhagavad Gītā, represented in diverse textual, devotional, and regional traditions; traditional narratives and historical questions are kept distinct.

title: Kuntī
description: The mother of the Pāṇḍavas, central to the Mahābhārata narrative; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Lakṣmaṇa
description: The devoted brother of Rāma in the Rāmāyaṇa; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Lakṣmī Forms
description: The eight principal forms of Lakṣmī (Aṣṭalakṣmī): Ādi, Dhana, Dhānya, Gaja, Santāna, Vīra, Vijaya, and Vidyā; their individual attributes, iconography, and the Aṣṭalakṣmī Stotram are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Lakṣmī
description: A goddess associated with prosperity, fortune, and Viṣṇu's consort in Vaiṣṇava traditions; represented here with attention to tradition-specific narratives.

title: Lalitā Sahasranāma
description: The Lalitā Sahasranāma (thousand names of Lalitā Tripurasundarī) from the Brahmanḍa Purāṇa, its dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya, and its centrality in Śrīvidyā and Śākta practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mādhyandina Śākhā
description: The Mādhyandina Śākhā is a principal recension of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda, prevalent in North India; its texts include the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahā Mrityunjaya Mantra
description: The Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (Ṛgveda 7.59.12), addressed to Tryambaka (Śiva), for conquering death and disease; its traditional use in healing, protection, and japa practice is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahābhārata Principal Characters
description: The principal characters of the Mahābhārata: the Pāṇḍavas (Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva), the Kauravas (Duryodhana and his brothers), Kṛṣṇa, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Draupadī, and others; their roles and relationships are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahābhārata Parvas
description: The eighteen parvas (books) of the Mahābhārata: Ādi, Sabhā, Araṇya, Virāṭa, Udyoga, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Śalya, Sauptika, Strī, Śānti, Anuśāsana, Āśramavāsika, Mausala, Mahāprasthānika, Svargārohaṇa; their narrative scope and key episodes are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahābhārata Upaniṣads
description: A group of Upaniṣads embedded in the Mahābhārata, including the Mokṣa-dharma-parvan and the Bhagavad Gītā context; their philosophical themes of dharma, mokṣa, and yoga are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahābhārata War
description: The Kurukṣetra War, the central conflict of the Mahābhārata, fought between the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas over eighteen days; its key warriors (Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Arjuna), the Bhagavad Gītā discourse, and its traditional dating are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahāpurāṇa
description: The eighteen major Purāṇas distinguished from the Upapurāṇas by their scope, authority, and coverage of the pañcalakṣaṇa.

title: Maitrāyaṇīya Śākhā
description: The Maitrāyaṇīya Śākhā is a recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; its texts include the Maitrāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka, and Upaniṣad; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mandodarī
description: The wife of Rāvaṇa in the Rāmāyaṇa, known for her wisdom and counsel; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Manuscript Catalogue
description: A systematic descriptive record of manuscript holdings, including codicological, paleographical, and textual metadata; its standards (TEI, MSDESC) and major projects are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Manuscript Preservation
description: The preventive and remedial conservation of manuscripts: environmental control, housing, handling, and treatment; its ethical principles and institutional practices are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Māyāvāda
description: The doctrine that the world is māyā (illusion), often used as a designation for Advaita by its critics; Advaitins typically prefer vivartavāda.

title: Māyā
description: A term for the power of manifestation or illusion, whose precise meaning varies significantly between Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, and Dvaita traditions.

title: Mīmāṃsā Apūrva
description: The Mīmāṃsā concept of apūrva (the unseen potency generated by ritual action that produces future fruits); its role in explaining the efficacy of Vedic rituals and the theory of karma are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mīmāṃsā Arthavāda
description: The Mīmāṃsā theory of arthavāda (explanatory passages in the Veda): the classification of Vedic sentences into vidhi (injunction), nṣedha (prohibition), and arthavāda (explanation); the three types of arthavāda — guṇavāda (eulogy), anuvāda (restatement), bhūtārthavāda (statement of fact) — and their hermeneutical role in ritual interpretation are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mīmāṃsā Dharma
description: The Mīmāṃsā conception of dharma as ritual duty prescribed by the Veda, known through śabda pramāṇa (verbal testimony); its distinction from laukika (worldly) dharma and its epistemological basis are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mīmāṃsā Sphoṭa
description: The Mīmāṃsā theory of sphoṭa (the eternal, unchanging word-essence) as the bearer of meaning, distinct from the audible sound (dhvani); the debate between Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (who rejects sphoṭa) and the Grammarians (who affirm it); the epistemological status of Vedic words and their relation to meaning are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mokṣa
description: A concept of liberation or release whose nature, means, and attainment are described in varied ways across traditions and texts.

title: Murugaṇ Forms
description: The forms of Murugaṇ (Kārttikeya, Subrahmaṇya, Skanda): the six-faced Ṣaṇmukha, the youthful Kumāra, the warrior Senāpati, the Tamil deity of the Kurinji landscape; the six abodes (Arupadai Veedu: Tiruttani, Swamimalai, Palani, Tirupparankunram, Pazhamudircholai, Tiruchendur); his iconography (vel, peacock, rooster) and the Kanda Shasti festival are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Navagraha
description: The Navagraha (nine celestial influencers): Sūrya (Sun), Candra (Moon), Maṅgala (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), Śukra (Venus), Śani (Saturn), Rāhu (ascending node), Ketu (descending node); their role in Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology), their temples (Navagraha sthalas), and their ritual propitiation (graha-śānti) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Nirukta
description: The Vedāṅga of etymology and semantic interpretation, exemplified by Yāska's Nirukta, which explains obscure Vedic terms.

title: Numismatics
description: The study of coins and currency for historical, economic, and cultural reconstruction; its Indian series and methodological approaches are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Nyāya Hetvābhāsa
description: The Nyāya classification of fallacies of inference (hetvābhāsas) including savyabhicāra, viruddha, satpratipakṣa, asiddha, and bādhita; their definitions and examples are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Nyāya Īśvara
description: The Nyāya concept of Īśvara (God) as the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe, the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the world, who is distinct from the material cause (prakṛti) and the individual selves (jīva); the arguments for God's existence (kārya-kāraṇa-anvaya, āyojanāt, dhṛtyādēḥ, padāt, pratyayataḥ, śrutēḥ) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Nyāya Pramāṇas
description: The Nyāya school recognizes four pramāṇas (means of valid knowledge): pratyakṣa (perception), anumāna (inference), upamāna (comparison), and śabda (verbal testimony); their definitions, scope, and interrelations are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Nyāya Siddhānta
description: The Nyāya school's core doctrines: the sixteen padārthas (categories) including pramāṇa (means of knowledge), prameya (objects of knowledge), saṃśaya (doubt), prayojana (purpose), dṛṣṭānta (example), siddhānta (tenet), avayava (members of inference), tarka (reasoning), nirṇaya (ascertainment), vāda (discussion), jalpa (wrangling), vitaṇḍā (cavil), hetvābhāsa (fallacies), chala (quibble), jāti (futile objection), and nigrahasthāna (point of defeat); their interrelations and epistemic significance are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya
description: The five-syllable Śaiva mantra (pañcākṣara) Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya, its centrality in Śaiva initiation and japa, and its occurrence in the Yajurveda (Śrī Rudram) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Oṃ Namo Nārāyaṇāya
description: The eight-syllable Vaiṣṇava mantra (aṣṭākṣara) Oṃ Namo Nārāyaṇāya, its role in Śrīvaiṣṇava initiation, and its connection to the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Oṃ
description: The praṇava or primordial syllable, discussed in Upaniṣads and foundational to Vedic and Tantric practice; represented here without reproducing esoteric instructions.

title: Padma Tīrtha
description: A sacred site associated with Viṣṇu's lotus (padma) manifestations; traditional accounts are represented without historical verification.

title: Paippalāda Śākhā
description: The Paippalāda Śākhā is a recension of the Atharvaveda, historically prominent in Kashmir and Odisha; its Saṃhitā is partially preserved and differs from the Śaunaka recension; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Paleography
description: The study of historical handwriting and scripts for dating, localizing, and reading manuscripts; its Indian script traditions (Brāhmī, Gupta, Śāradā, etc.) are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Pañcamahābhūta
description: The five great elements (pañcamahābhūta) in Vedic and Sāṃkhya cosmology: ākāśa (space/ether), vāyu (air), agni (fire), jala/ap (water), pṛthvī (earth); their subtle essences (tanmātras: śabda, sparśa, rūpa, rasa, gandha), their sequence of manifestation, and their correspondence to sense organs are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Pariṇāmavāda
description: The doctrine of "real transformation" — the world as a genuine modification (pariṇāma) of Brahman or prakṛti, upheld by Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, and Sāṃkhya.

title: Prakṛti
description: In Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the material principle composed of the three guṇas; in other contexts, a term for nature or the material world.

title: Prasthānatraya
description: The "three foundations" of Vedānta: the Upaniṣads (śruti-prasthāna), the Brahma Sūtras (nyāya-prasthāna), and the Bhagavad Gītā (smṛti-prasthāna).

title: Prāyaścitta Types
description: The classification of prāyaścitta (expiation) in Dharmaśātra: prāṇāyāma, tīrtha-yātrā, dāna, vrata, homa, japa, and fasting; their application to specific offenses (pātaka, upapātaka) and the gradation of penances are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Prāyaścitta
description: Expiatory rites prescribed in Dharmaśāstra for intentional or unintentional transgressions; their forms and severity vary by text and offense.

title: Pūjā Ṣoḍaśopacāra
description: The sixteen upacāras (offerings) in formal Pūjā: āvāhana (invocation), āsana (seat), pādyā (water for feet), arghya (water for hands), ācamana (sipping water), snāna (bath), vastra (clothing), yajñopavīta (sacred thread), gandha (sandalwood), puṣpa (flowers), dhūpa (incense), dīpa (lamp), naivedya (food), tāmbūla (betel), nīrājana (waving lights), and mantra-puṣpāñjali; their sequence and significance are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahāpurāṇa List
description: The eighteen Mahāpurāṇas: Brahma, Padma, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Liṅga, Garuḍa, Nārada, Bhāgavata, Agni, Skanda, Bhaviṣya, Brahmāṇḍa, Vāmana, Kūrma, Matsya, Vāyu, Varāha, and Vāyu; their traditional enumeration and thematic groupings are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Purāṇa Pañcalakṣaṇa
description: The five distinguishing characteristics of a Purāṇa: sarga (creation), pratisarga (re-creation), vaṃśa (genealogy), manvantara (cosmic ages), and vaṃśānucarita (dynastic history).

title: Purāṇa Sectarian Classification
description: The traditional tripartite classification of Purāṇas by predominance of guṇas: Sāttvika (Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa), Rājasa (Brahmā), and Tāmasa (Śiva); this classification's textual basis and sectarian implications are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Purāṇa Structure
description: The five characteristic topics (pañcalakṣaṇa) of the Purāṇas: sarga (creation), pratisarga (secondary creation), vaṃśa (genealogies), manvantara (cosmic cycles), and vaṃśānucarita (dynastic histories); their textual manifestation across the Purāṇic corpus is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Purāṇa Traditional Attribution
description: Traditional attribution assigns the major Purāṇas to Vyāsa as compiler; this attribution is represented here as a traditional claim distinct from modern textual scholarship on Purāṇa composition and stratification. ---

title: Upapurāṇas
description: The eighteen Upapurāṇas (minor Purāṇas): Saura, Nṛsiṃha, Viṣṇu Dharmottara, Kālikā, Garga, Āditya, Nandi, Sāmba, Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya, Bhārgava, Matsya, Varāha, Kapila, Mānava, Auśanasa, Sāmba, Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya, and Bhārgava; their relationship to the Mahāpurāṇas and their distinct thematic foci are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Puruṣa
description: In Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the conscious principle distinct from prakṛti; in Vedic and Vedāntic contexts, a term for the cosmic person or the self.

title: Puruṣārtha
description: The four recognized aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa—whose relative priority and interpretation vary by textual tradition and stage of life.

title: Rājadharma
description: The Dharmaśāstra conception of rājadharma (kingly duties): the king's role as protector of varṇāśrama-dharma, the principles of just rule (daṇḍanīti), taxation, justice, and the ideal of the cakravartin; its textual exposition in Smṛti and Arthaśāstra traditions is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Rāma Forms
description: The forms of Rāma: the prince of Ayodhyā, the exiled forest-dweller, the victor over Rāvaṇa, the ideal king (Rāmarājya), and the supreme Parabrahman (in Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa); his iconography (bow, arrow, accompanied by Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, Hanumān), and his worship in the Rāmānandī and Rāmānuja traditions are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Rāma
description: A central figure of the Rāmāyaṇa, represented in textual, devotional, and performative traditions; this record does not conflate traditional narratives with historical biography.

title: Rāmāyaṇa Principal Characters
description: The principal characters of the Rāmāyaṇa: Rāma, Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna, Hanumān, Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāvaṇa, and others; their roles and relationships are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Rāmāyaṇa Kāṇḍas
description: The seven kāṇḍas (books) of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa: Bāla, Ayodhyā, Araṇya, Kiṣkindhā, Sundara, Yuddha, Uttara; their narrative structure and key episodes are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Rāmāyaṇa Philosophy
description: The philosophical and ethical teachings of the Rāmāyaṇa: the ideals of dharma (righteousness), satya (truth), kṣamā (forgiveness), dayā (compassion), and the ideal ruler (Rāma-rājya); the roles of ideal son, brother, husband, and king as embodied by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Rāṇāyanīya Śākhā
description: The Rāṇāyanīya Śākhā is a recension of the Sāmaveda, historically prominent in Gujarat and Maharashtra; its texts are closely related to the Kauthuma recension; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Rasa Siddhānta
description: The aesthetic theory of "rasa" (aesthetic sentiment) systematized in the Nāṭyaśāstra, with its eight/nine rasas and the conditions of their evocation; represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Rāvaṇa
description: The antagonist of the Rāmāyaṇa, ruler of Laṅkā; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Recension
description: A distinct version or redaction of a text transmitted in a particular geographical, textual, or institutional tradition; its identification and classification are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Ṛgveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Ṛgveda: the Śākalya śākhā (the only complete surviving recension), and historically attested lost recensions such as Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, and Māṇḍukeya; their textual differences and geographical distribution are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Ṛṇa-trayā
description: The three debts (ṛṇa-traya) in Dharmaśāstra: ṛṣi-ṛṇa (debt to sages, repaid by study), deva-ṛṇa (debt to gods, repaid by sacrifice), pitṛ-ṛṇa (debt to ancestors, repaid by progeny); their textual basis and role in householder life are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Ṛṇa
description: The "three debts" — to ṛṣis (via study), to devas (via sacrifice), to pitṛs (via progeny) — that frame human obligation in Dharmaśāstra.

title: Śrī Rudram
description: The Śrī Rudram (Śatarudrīya) from the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda), its eleven anuvākas, the Namakam and Chamakam sections, and its use in Śiva worship and abhiṣeka are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śākta Tantras
description: The Śākta Tantras: the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra, Kulārṇava Tantra, Rudrayāmala, Brahmayāmala, and the Śrīvidyā tradition (Tripurā Rahasya, Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava); their doctrine of the Goddess as supreme (Śakti/Devī), the śrīcakra, the ten Mahāvidyās, and the kuṇḍalinī yoga; their role in Śrīvidyā upāsanā and temple ritual are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Sāmaveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Sāmaveda: Kauthuma (the principal surviving recension), Rāṇāyanīya, and Jaiminīya/Talavakāra; their melodic differences and geographical distribution are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Saṃsāra
description: The cyclic process of birth, death, and rebirth that provides the soteriological background for the pursuit of liberation in Indian traditions.

title: Saṃskāra Types
description: The sixteen principal saṃskāras (sacraments) in Dharmaśāstra: garbhādhāna (conception), puṃsavana (ensuring male offspring), sīmantonnayana (parting hair), jātakarma (birth), nāmakaraṇa (naming), niṣkramaṇa (first outing), annaprāśana (first solid food), cūḍākaraṇa (tonsure), upanayana (sacred thread), vedārambha (Vedic study), keśānta (first shaving), samāvartana (completion of studies), vivāha (marriage), and antyeṣṭi (funeral); their timing, mantras, and social significance are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Sāṃkhya Evolution (Parinama)
description: The Sāṃkhya theory of cosmic evolution (pariṇāma) from prakṛti: the sequential manifestation of mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra (ego), the five tanmātras (subtle elements), the five mahābhūtas (gross elements), the five jñānendriyas (sense organs), the five karmendriyas (action organs), and manas (mind); the teleological direction of evolution toward the liberation of puruṣa is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Sāṃkhya Guṇatraya
description: The three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) as the constituent strands of prakṛti in Sāṃkhya philosophy; their characteristics, interactions, and role in cosmic evolution and bondage are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Sāṃkhya Puruṣa-Prakṛti
description: The Sāṃkhya dualism of puruṣa (pure consciousness, plural, passive witness) and prakṛti (primordial matter, singular, active, composed of three guṇas); their interaction (saṃyoga) as the cause of evolution, the distinction between knowledge (jñāna) and ignorance (ajñāna), and liberation (kaivalya) as the isolation of puruṣa from prakṛti are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Sāṃkhya Tattvas
description: The Sāṃkhya enumeration of twenty-five tattvas (principles): prakṛti (primordial matter), mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra, five tanmātras, five mahābhūtas, five jñānendriyas, five karmendriyas, manas, and puruṣa (consciousness); their evolutionary sequence and interrelations are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Saṃnyāsa
description: Saṃnyāsa (renunciation): the fourth āśrama (stage of life) in Dharmaśāstra, characterized by the renunciation of worldly duties, the adoption of the ochre robe (kāṣāya), the begging bowl (bhikṣāpātra), and the pursuit of mokṣa through jñāna and vairāgya; the types of saṃnyāsa (kuṭīcaka, bahūdaka, haṃsa, paramahaṃsa), the saṃnyāsa dīkṣā, and the saṃnyāsī's daily routine are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Saptarṣi
description: The Saptarṣi (seven sages): the seven primordial sages (Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha) who are the mind-born sons of Brahmā, the authors of Vedic hymns, and the progenitors of gotras; their astronomical identification with the Ursa Major constellation (Saptarṣi Maṇḍala) and their role in Vedic tradition are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Sarasvatī Forms
description: The forms of Sarasvatī: Vāc (speech), Bhāratī (eloquence), Śāradā (autumn goddess), and Vāṇī (voice); her iconography with vīṇā, pustaka, and haṃsa, and her role as goddess of knowledge, arts, and learning are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Sarasvatī
description: A goddess associated with learning, speech, and the arts; also the name of a Vedic river whose identification is debated in scholarship and tradition.

title: Śaunaka Śākhā
description: The Śaunaka Śākhā is the principal surviving recension of the Atharvaveda; its texts include the Atharvaveda Saṃhitā, Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, and several Upaniṣads; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śaiva Āgamas
description: The twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas (e.g., Kāmika, Kāraṇa, Suprabheda, Raurava, Mṛgendra, Sarvokta, Pārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Vātula, Parameśvara) and their upāgamas; their fourfold structure (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā), their doctrine of Śiva-Śakti, the pāśa (bondage) and mokṣa; their role in temple construction, daily worship, and initiation are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śikṣā
description: The Vedāṅga concerned with phonetics, pronunciation, and euphonic combination; its treatises form the foundation for Vedic recitation.

title: Śilpa Śāstra
description: The traditional Indian system of iconography and sculpture, prescribing proportions, gestures, attributes, and materials for deity images; its texts and regional schools are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śrāddha Types
description: The types of śrāddha (ancestral rites) in Dharmaśāstra: nitya (daily), naimittika (occasional), kāmya (desire-motivated), and the specific rites like sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, saparvaṇa, ekodiṣṭa; their performers, timing, and offerings are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śruti
description: Śruti (that which is heard): the authoritative revealed texts of Hinduism, comprising the four Vedas (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, Atharva) and their associated Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas, and Upaniṣads; distinguished from Smṛti (remembered tradition); its apauruṣeya (non-human authorship) status, its role as the ultimate pramāṇa in orthodox schools, and its oral transmission (paramparā) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śuddhādvaita Puṣṭi
description: In Śuddhādvaita Vedānta (Vallabha), puṣṭi (grace) is the unmerited divine favor that enables the soul's participation in Kṛṣṇa's līlā; the puṣṭi-mārga (path of grace) and its distinction from the maryādā-mārga (path of law) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Siglum
description: A conventional symbol or abbreviation identifying a specific manuscript witness in a critical apparatus; its assignment and notation standards are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Sītā
description: The wife of Rāma, central to the Rāmāyaṇa; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Smṛti
description: Smṛti (that which is remembered): the body of post-Vedic authoritative texts including the Dharmaśāstras (Manusmṛti, Yājñavalkyasmṛti), the Itihāsas (Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa), the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Vedāṅgas; distinguished from Śruti (revealed) as being of human authorship but traditionally authoritative; its role in prescribing dharma, ritual, and social order is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śrīmad Bhāgavata Commentary Traditions
description: The diverse commentarial traditions on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, including Śrīdhara Svāmī, Jīva Gosvāmī, Viśvanātha Cakravartī, and others; represented as a catalogue entry.

title: Stemmatics
description: The method of reconstructing manuscript genealogies (stemma codicum) to infer textual relationships; its principles, limitations, and computational approaches are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Strīdharmā
description: The body of Dharmaśāstra prescriptions concerning women's duties and rites; textual prescriptions are distinguished from diverse historical and regional practices.

title: Sūrya Navagraha
description: Sūrya as the chief of the Navagraha (nine planets), his iconography (seven-horse chariot, Aruṇa as charioteer), the Sūrya mantras, and his role in Vedic and Jyotiṣa traditions are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Taittirīya Śākhā
description: The Taittirīya Śākhā is the principal surviving recension of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda, prevalent in South India; its texts include the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka, and Upaniṣad; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Tantra Śāstra
description: The Tantra Śāstra corpus: the textual tradition of Tantra (Śākta, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist), characterized by ritual (kriyā), meditation (yoga), mantra, yantra, maṇḍala, and the guru-śiṣya transmission; its distinction from Vedic orthopraxy (smārta), its esoteric (guhya) nature, and its influence on temple ritual, iconography, and popular practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Tantra
description: Tantra: the esoteric ritual and yogic tradition transmitted through guru-śiṣya lineages, characterized by the use of mantra, yantra, maṇḍala, dīkṣā (initiation), and the worship of deities in their fierce and benign forms; its textual corpus (Tantras, Āgamas, Saṃhitās), its distinction from Vedic smārta practice, and its influence on temple ritual, iconography, and popular practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Textual Criticism
description: The discipline of evaluating manuscript variants to reconstruct a text's history and establish an edited text; its methods (stemmatics, best-text, cladistics) are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Thumri and Dadra
description: The light classical forms of Hindustani music: thumrī (romantic, erotic, based on Braj/Hindi poetry, set to dīpacandī/punjabi tāl), dadra (lighter, faster, in dadra tāl), kājrī, caitī, horī; their gharanā styles (Purab, Punjab), their place in the concert format after khayāl, and their emotive (śṛṅgāra) content are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Tīrtha Types
description: The classification of tīrtha (pilgrimage sites) in Purāṇic and Dharmaśāstra tradition: deva-tīrtha (deity-associated), ṛṣi-tīrtha (sage-associated), mṛtyu-tīrtha (death-related), and the distinction between mukti-tīrtha (liberation-granting) and bhukti-tīrtha (enjoyment-granting); their ritual protocols are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Trisandhyā
description: The trisandhyā (three daily junctions): the Vedic prescription for worship at dawn (prātaḥ-sandhyā), noon (mādhyāhnika), and dusk (sāyaṃ-sandhyā); the Gāyatrī mantra recitation, prāṇāyāma, arghya offering, and upasthāna; its role in the daily routine of the twice-born (dvija) and its continuation in modern practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vairāgya
description: Dispassion or non-attachment, presented in texts as a prerequisite for contemplative progress, with degrees and nuances described differently across traditions.

title: Vaiśeṣika Atomism
description: The Vaiśeṣika atomic theory positing four kinds of eternal, indivisible atoms (paramāṇu) — earth, water, fire, air — each with distinct qualities (guṇa); their binary combinations (dvyanuka) and ternary combinations (tryanuka) forming the gross physical world; the theory's differences from Greek atomism and its role in Vaiśeṣika physics are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vaiśeṣika Creation Theory
description: The Vaiśeṣika theory of creation (sṛṣṭi) and dissolution (pralaya) through the combination and separation of eternal atoms (paramāṇu) guided by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) of individual selves; the atomic structure of the four physical elements (earth, water, fire, air) and the non-atomic substances (space, time, direction, mind, self) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vaiśeṣika Padārthas
description: The Vaiśeṣika school enumerates seven padārthas (categories of existence): dravya (substance), guṇa (quality), karma (action), sāmānya (generality), viśeṣa (particularity), samavāya (inherence), and abhāva (absence); their definitions and interrelations are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vaiśeṣika Paramāṇu
description: The Vaiśeṣika atomic theory (paramāṇu-vāda) positing eternal, indivisible atoms as the ultimate constituents of physical substances; its metaphysical implications and differences from other atomic theories are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vaiṣṇava Āgamas
description: The Vaiṣṇava Āgamas: the Pāñcarātra corpus (e.g., Jayākhya, Ahirbudhnya, Paushkara, Sāttvata) and the Vaikhānasa texts; their doctrine of Viṣṇu's five forms (para, vyūha, vibhava, antaryāmin, arcā), the fivefold daily worship (pañcakāla), and their influence on temple ritual in Śrīvaiṣṇava and other traditions are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Varṇa-āśrama Dharma
description: The integrated system of varṇa (four social classes) and āśrama (four life stages) duties in Dharmaśāstra; the interdependence of social and life-stage obligations, their textual basis in Smṛti texts, and their role in traditional society are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Varṇa
description: The fourfold classification—brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra—whose textual prescriptions, historical manifestations, and contemporary significance are distinct and should not be conflated.

title: Vāstu Śāstra
description: The traditional Indian system of architecture and spatial design, governing temple, palace, and domestic construction; its texts, principles, and regional variations are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vedic Cosmology
description: Vedic cosmology: the Ṛgvedic vision of the universe (brahmāṇḍa) emerging from the cosmic sacrifice (puruṣa-sūkta, RV 10.90), the three worlds (bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ), the cosmic mountain (Meru), the seven dvīpas and oceans; the Upaniṣadic evolution to brahman as the substrate of all; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vedic Deities
description: The principal Vedic deities: Agni (fire), Indra (rain/warrior), Varuṇa (cosmic order), Mitra (contracts), the Aśvins (healing), Sūrya/Savitṛ (sun), Uṣas (dawn), Vāyu (wind), Rudra (storm), Viṣṇu (strides), Pūṣan (paths), Bṛhaspati (priesthood); their hymns, functions, and evolution into later Hindu deities are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vedic Mantra Classification
description: The classification of Vedic mantras: ṛc (Ṛgveda verses), yajus (Yajurveda prose), sāman (Sāmaveda chants), nigada (loud recitation); the division into mantra and brāhmaṇa portions; the gāyatrī, uṣṇik, anuṣṭubh, bṛhatī, paṅkti, triṣṭubh, jagatī metres; the distinction between mantra and bhāṣya are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vedic Metre (Chandas)
description: The system of Vedic metres (chandas): gāyatrī (24 syllables), uṣṇik (28), anuṣṭubh (32), bṛhatī (36), paṅkti (40), triṣṭubh (44), jagatī (48), and their use in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā; the transition to classical Sanskrit metres is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vedic Priesthood (Ṛtvij)
description: The four principal Vedic priests (ṛtvij) and their assistants: hotṛ (Ṛgveda recitation), adhvaryu (Yajurveda ritual action), udgātṛ (Sāmaveda chanting), brahman (Atharvaveda supervision); their roles, assistants, and the symbolic correspondence to the four Vedas are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vedic Ritual (Yajña)
description: The Vedic sacrificial system (yajña): the seven havir-yajñas (Agnihotra, Darśa-pūrṇamāsa, Āgrayaṇa, Cāturmāsya, Nirūḍhapaśubandha, Sautrāmaṇi, Agniṣṭoma) and the seven soma-yajñas (Agnistoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, Aptoryāma); their structure, priests (ṛtvij), and cosmological significance are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vedic Time Cycles
description: Vedic and post-Vedic time cycles: the four yugas (Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali) and their durations (4:3:2:1), the mahāyuga (4.32 million years), the manvantara (71 mahāyugas), the kalpa (1000 mahāyugas = 4.32 billion years), Brahmā's day and night; their Puranic elaboration and traditional cosmological significance are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Videhamukti
description: Liberation after death, contrasted with jīvanmukti; its relationship to embodied liberation varies across Vedānta schools.

title: Vidura
description: The wise half-brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, known for his counsel in the Mahābhārata; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Viśiṣṭādvaita Nitya-vibhūti
description: In Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta, nitya-vibhūti (eternal manifestation) is the spiritual realm of Vaikuṇṭha, distinct from the material world (līlā-vibhūti); its nature as the abode of the released souls and the eternal sport of Viṣṇu is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Viśiṣṭādvaita Prapatti
description: In Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta, prapatti (śaraṇāgati) is the act of complete self-surrender to Viṣṇu as the sole means to liberation; its six limbs (ānikūlya-varjana, ānukūlya-saṅkalpa, rakṣiṣyatīti-viśvāsa, goptṛtva-varaṇa, ātma-nikṣepa, kārpaṇya) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Viṣṇu Sahasranāma
description: The Viṣṇu Sahasranāma (thousand names of Viṣṇu) from the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsana Parva), recited by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira; its structure, key names (Viśveśvara, Viṣṇu, Vāṣṭakāra), and role in daily recitation are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vivartavāda
description: The Advaita doctrine of "apparent manifestation" — the world as an illusory appearance (vivarta) of Brahman, not a real transformation.

title: Vrata Categories
description: The classification of vrata (vows/observances) in Smṛti and Purāṇic tradition: nitya (daily), naimittika (occasion-specific), kāmya (desire-motivated), the upavāsa (fasting) types, the kāla-vratas (time-based), and the kāyika-vācika-mānasa distinction; their role in purification and merit are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vrata Dharma
description: The role of vrata (vowed observance) in Dharmaśāstra: the classification into nitya (daily), naimittika (occasion-specific), and kāmya (desire-motivated); the components of vrata (saṅkalpa, upavāsa, japa, dāna, pūjā); its role in purification, merit (puṇya), and the attainment of specific goals are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Vyākaraṇa
description: The Vedāṅga of grammar, epitomized by Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, which systematized Sanskrit morphology and syntax.

title: Vyavahāra
description: The Dharmaśāstra category of vyavahāra (legal procedure): the courts, evidence (pramāṇa), types of disputes (vivāda), punishments (daṇḍa), and the procedural rules for litigation; its exposition in Manusmṛti, Yājñavalkya Smṛti, and later digests is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yajña Types
description: The classification of yajña in Vedic and Smṛta tradition: nitya (daily, like agnihotra), naimittika (occasional), kāmya (desire-motivated), the seven havir-yajñas, the seven soma-yajñas, and the mahāyajñas (panca-mahāyajña); their performers, materials, and purposes are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yajurveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Yajurveda: Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda śākhās — Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇīya, Kaṭha, Kāpiṣṭhala — and Śukla (White) Yajurveda śākhās — Mādhyandina and Kāṇva; their structural differences (Saṃhitā/Brāhmaṇa separation vs. intermingling) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yoga Aṣṭāṅga
description: The eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) of Patañjali's Yoga: yama (restraints), niyama (observances), āsana (posture), prāṇāyāma (breath control), pratyāhāra (sense withdrawal), dhāraṇā (concentration), dhyāna (meditation), samādhi (absorption); their sequential practice and interdependence are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yoga Kleśas
description: The five kleśas (afflictions) in Patañjali's Yoga: avidyā (ignorance), asmitā (egoism), rāga (attachment), dveṣa (aversion), abhiniveśa (fear of death); their role in saṃsāra and their removal through yogic practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yoga Nidrā
description: Yoga Nidrā (yogic sleep): a guided relaxation and meditation technique leading to a state of conscious deep sleep between waking and sleeping; its roots in the tantric tradition (nyāsa), its modern systematization (Satyananda Saraswati), and its therapeutic applications are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yoga Samādhi
description: The Yoga concept of samādhi (absorption): the stages of saṃprajñāta (with cognitive content — vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, asmitā) and asaṃprajñāta (without cognitive content, nirbīja); the distinction between sabīja (with seed) and nirbīja (seedless) samādhi, and the role of dispassion (vairāgya) and practice (abhyāsa) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yoga Samāpatti
description: The state of samāpatti (coalescence) in Patañjali's Yoga, where the mind becomes transparent like a crystal reflecting the object of meditation; its stages (vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, asmitā) and relation to samādhi are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yoga Viveka-khyāti
description: The Yoga concept of viveka-khyāti (discriminative knowledge) as the direct intuitive realization of the distinction between puruṣa (consciousness) and prakṛti (matter); its attainment through the practice of the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) leading to kaivalya (liberation); its distinction from mere intellectual understanding are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Yoga
description: A term with philosophical, contemplative and practical uses across different traditions; it is not reduced here to one modern meaning.

title: Yudhiṣṭhira
description: The eldest Pāṇḍava, known for his adherence to dharma; traditional narratives are represented without historical conflation.

title: Āyurveda
description: The traditional Indian system of medicine, with its textual foundations (Caraka, Suśruta, Vāgbhaṭa), tridoṣa theory, and therapeutic modalities; represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Bhārata Nāṭyam
description: The classical dance form of Tamil Nadu, reconstructed in the 20th century from sadir traditions; its repertoire (alarippu, jatisvaram, varṇam, padam, tillāṇa) and theoretical basis are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Bidriware
description: Bidriware, the metal handicraft of Bidar (Karnataka), characterized by silver inlay on a blackened zinc-copper alloy; its Persian origins (14th century), motifs (floral, geometric, calligraphic), and products (vases, boxes, jewelry); its GI tag and contemporary revival are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Karnāṭaka Saṅgīta
description: Karnāṭaka Saṅgīta (कर्नाटक संगीत / கர்நாடக சங்கீதம் / കർണാടക സംഗീതం), the classical music tradition of South India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana). Core: rāga (melodic framework), tāḷa (rhythmic cycle), and compositional forms — varṇam, kṛti, tillāṇa, javali, padam, svarajati. The Trinity (18th-19th c.): Tyāgarāja (kṛti perfection, bhakti), Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar (Sanskrit, śrī vidyā, western notes), Śyāma Śāstri (Svarajati, Kāmākṣi). Pedagogy: sarali varisai, jaṇṭai varisai, daṭṭu varisai, alankāram, gītaṃ, svarajati, varṇam, kṛti. The 72 melakarta rāga system (Venkatamakhin). Instruments: vīṇā, veṇu, violin, mṛdaṅgam, ghaṭam, kanjira, morsing. The December Music Season (Chennai) is the world's largest classical music festival. --- The classical music tradition of South India, with its rāga, tāḷa, and compositional forms (kṛti, varṇam, tillāṇa); its history, composers (Tyāgarāja, Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar, Śyāma Śāstri), and pedagogy are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Citrakalā
description: The diverse painting traditions of India: mural (Ajanta, Ellora), miniature (Mughal, Rajput, Pahari, Deccani), folk (Madhubani, Warli, Pattachitra); represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Dhanurveda
description: The traditional Indian science of archery and warfare, counted as an Upaveda; its texts, techniques, and historical practice are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Dokra Art
description: The Dokra (Dhokra) non-ferrous metal casting tradition of the tribal communities of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, and Odisha; the lost-wax casting technique (cire perdue) creating brass/bronze figurines of deities, animals, and daily life; its ancient origins (Harappan), ritual use, and contemporary market adaptation are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gāndharva Veda
description: The traditional Indian science of music and performing arts, counted as an Upaveda; its theoretical foundations and relationship to the Nāṭyaśāstra are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Hindustānī Saṅgīta
description: The classical music tradition of North India, with its rāga, tāḷa, and forms (dhrupad, khayāl, ṭhumrī); its gharanās, composers, and historical development are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kalamkari Painting
description: The Kalamkari (pen-craft) painting tradition of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam styles); hand-painted or block-printed cotton textiles with natural dyes depicting Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata, and Purāṇic themes; its Persian influence and contemporary revival are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kāṭhakaḷi
description: Kāṭhakaḷi (കഥകളി), Kerala's classical dance-drama (17th century synthesis of Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam, Rāmanāṭṭam, and folk traditions). Key elements: elaborate vesham (makeup/costume) — paccā (green, noble), kaṭṭi (knife, anti-hero), kari (black, demoness), taṭi (beard: white=divine, red=evil, black=hunter), minukku (radiant, female/sage); the navarasas (nine emotions) through facial muscles (netrābhinaya); the āṭṭakathās (scripts) from Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, Bhāgavata (e.g., Nalacaritam, Kalyāṇasaugandhikam); sopāna-saṅgīta (Sopana music) with ceṇḍa, maṭalam, elathāḷam; rigorous gurukula training (8-10 years) at Kala Mandalam, Kottakkal. Recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. A synthesis of nṛtya (dance), nṛtta (pure movement), and nāṭya (drama). --- The classical dance-drama tradition of Kerala, with elaborate costume, makeup, and facial expressions; its repertoire (āṭṭakathās), music, and training system are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Kucipuḍi
description: The classical dance-drama tradition of Andhra Pradesh, with solo and group forms; its history, repertoire, and theoretical basis are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Madhubani Painting
description: The Madhubani (Mithila) painting tradition of Bihar, characterized by geometric patterns, natural dyes, and ritual themes; its wall-painting origins, women's practice, and contemporary paper/canvas adaptation are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Manipuri
description: The classical dance tradition of Manipur, with its devotional themes (Rāsa Līlā), subtle movements, and distinctive costume; its repertoire and ritual context are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Meenakari
description: Meenakari (enamelling), the art of decorating metal surfaces (gold, silver, copper) with colored enamel; its Persian origins, centers in Jaipur, Udaipur, Delhi, and Varanasi; its application on jewelry, weapons, and decorative objects; the champlevé and cloisonné techniques are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mohiniyāṭṭam
description: Mohiniyāṭṭam (മോഹിനിയാട്ടം), Kerala's classical solo dance (lasya style), traditionally performed by women. Reconstructed in the 1930s by V.N. Menon and Kala Mandalam (Vallathol Narayana Menon, Mukundraj). Key elements: graceful circular movements (cuzhippu), swaying gait (gamana), subtle facial expressions (sāttvika abhinaya), white/cream costume with gold border (kasavu), jasmine hair adornment. The repertoire: colkeṭṭu (invocation), jati-svaram, varṇam, padam, tillānā. Music: Sopana style, Carnatic rāgas (Tōḍi, Bhairavi, Kalyāṇi), accompaniment: veena, veṇu, maddaḷam, eḷattāḷam. Themes: Śṛṅgāra (love), Bhakti (devotion to Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa). Mohinī = Viṣṇu's enchantress form (distributing amṛta). Recognized by Sangeet Natak Akademi. --- The classical solo dance tradition of Kerala, characterized by graceful circular movements and feminine expression; its repertoire and historical reconstruction are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Oḍissī
description: The classical dance tradition of Odisha, reconstructed from mahārī and gotipuā traditions; its repertoire, sculpturesque poses, and theoretical basis are represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Pahari Miniature Painting
description: The Pahari miniature painting schools of the Himalayan foothills: Basohli (bold colors, geometric), Kangra (lyrical, naturalistic), Guler, Chamba, Mandi, Kullu, and Jammu; their themes (Gīta Govinda, Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Nala-Damayantī, portraits), the delicate lines, soft colors, and their refinement of the Mughal style are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Pattachitra Painting
description: The Pattachitra cloth painting tradition of Odisha and West Bengal, characterized by bold lines, natural colors, and themes from Jagannātha cult, Rāmāyaṇa, and Mahābhārata; its ritual use in temple worship is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Pichwai Painting
description: The Pichwai painting tradition of Nathdwara (Rajasthan), large cloth paintings hung behind the Śrīnāthajī deity (Kṛṣṇa as seven-year-old); their seasonal themes (Śarad Pūrṇimā, Gopāṣṭamī, Annakūṭa), use of natural pigments, and ritual function in the Puṣṭimārga tradition are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Rajasthani Miniature Painting
description: The Rajasthani miniature painting schools: Mewar (Udaipur), Marwar (Jodhpur), Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh, Jaipur, and Bikaner; their themes (Rāgamālā, Rasikapriyā, Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Rāmāyaṇa, court portraits), the use of natural pigments, the bold lines and vibrant colors, and their Mughal influence are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Saṃskṛta Nāṭya
description: The classical Sanskrit theatre tradition, with its nāṭyaśāstra foundation, dramatic types (nāṭaka, prakaraṇa), and playwrights (Kālidāsa, Bhāsa, Śūdraka, Bhavabhūti); represented here as a catalogue entry.

title: Thanjavur Painting
description: The Thanjavur (Tanjore) painting tradition of Tamil Nadu, characterized by gold leaf, vibrant colors, and gesso work; its themes (Śrī Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Rāma), technique, and patronage by Maratha rulers are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Warli Painting
description: The Warli painting tradition of the Warli tribe (Maharashtra–Gujarat border), characterized by white geometric figures on mud walls depicting daily life, nature, and rituals; its ritual origins (marriage, harvest), the use of rice paste, and its contemporary adaptation to paper/canvas are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Ayyappan
description: Ayyappan (അയ്യപ്പന്‍ / ஐயப்பன்), also Śāstā, Hariharaputra, Dharma-Śāstā — the deity of Sabarimala, born from the union of Śiva and Viṣṇu (as Mohinī). Embodies the synthesis of Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava traditions. Key attributes: celibacy (naiṣṭhika brahmacarya), the 18 holy steps (paṭinēṭṭāmpaṭi / பதினெட்டாம்படி), the 41-day vrata (maṇḍala kālam / மண்டல காலம்) with strict observances (black/blue clothes, no shaving, brahmacarya, daily bath). The pilgrimage to Sabarimala (Kerala) draws 40-50 million annually (Nov-Jan). The Makaravilakku (Makara Jyoti) on Makara Saṅkrānti is the climax. Worshipped across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and beyond. The Vāvaru (Muslim devotee) shrine at Erumeli exemplifies communal harmony. ---

title: Devī
description: Devī (देवी / தேவி / ਦੇਵੀ / ദേവি / দেবী), the Goddess, Śakti, Ambikā, Durgā, Pārvatī, Kālī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Mahiṣāsuramardinī, Caṇḍikā, Annapūrṇā, Kāmākṣī, Mīnākṣī. Central to Śākta traditions (Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, Durgā Pūjā). The Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptashatī, Caṇḍī-pāṭha) is the foundational text. Manifestations: Navadurgā (9 forms), Daśamahāvidyā (10 wisdom goddesses), Aṣṭalakṣmī (8 Lakṣmīs). Consort of Śiva (Pārvatī), Viṣṇu (Lakṣmī), Brahmā (Sarasvatī). Festivals: Navarātrī/Durgā Pūjā, Vasanta Navarātrī, Kālī Pūjā, Lakṣmī Pūjā, Sarasvatī Pūjā. Śākta Pīṭhas: 51/108 sites (Kāmākhyā, Kālikā, Jvālāmukhī, Viśālākṣī). --- The Goddess in her manifold forms; this record represents the broad category of Devī-centered traditions without collapsing their distinct textual and ritual expressions.

title: Gaṇeśa
description: Gaṇeśa (गणेश / விநாயகர் / గణేష్ / ಗಣೇಶ / ഗണപതി / গণেশ / ગણેશ), Vināyaka, Piḷḷaiyār, Vighneśvara, Gajānanā — the elephant-headed deity, remover of obstacles (Vighnahartā), lord of beginnings. Son of Śiva and Pārvatī. Consorts: Siddhi (success), Buddhi (wisdom); or Ṛddhi/Siddhi. Vehicle: Mūṣaka (mouse). Attributes: broken tusk (ekadanta), modaka (sweet), axe, noose. Key texts: Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, Mudgala Purāṇa, Gaṇeśa Atharvaśīrṣa. Worshipped first in all rituals. Festivals: Gaṇeśa Caturthī (Bhādrapada Śukla Caturthī), Vināyaka Caturthī, Saṅkaṣṭī Caturthī (monthly). Regional: Mumbai's Lalbaugcha Raja, Pune's Dagdusheth, Tamil Nadu's Piḷḷaiyārpatti, Kerala's Koṭṭārakkara. --- A widely revered deity whose iconography, narratives, and ritual roles vary across regions, texts, and devotional communities.

title: Narasiṃha
description: Narasiṃha, the man-lion avatar of Viṣṇu, whose emergence from the pillar to protect Prahlāda and slay Hiraṇyakaśipu is a central Vaiṣṇava narrative; his iconography, temples, and worship traditions are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Pārvatī
description: Pārvatī (Umā), the consort of Śiva and the embodiment of Śakti, her forms as Durgā, Kālī, Annapūrṇā, and Gaurī; her role as mother of Gaṇeśa and Skanda, and her worship across Śākta and Śaiva traditions are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Śiva
description: Śiva (शिव / சிவன் / ಶಿವ / ശിവന്‍ / শিব / શિવ), the Auspicious One, Maheśvara, Rudra, Paśupati, Nīlakaṇṭha, Naṭarāja (cosmic dancer), Dakṣiṇāmūrti (guru), Ardhanārīśvara (half-female). Central to Śaiva traditions (Śaiva Siddhānta, Kashmir Śaivism, Vīraśaivism, Liṅgāyat). The liṅga (aniconic form) is the primary worship focus. Twelve Jyotirliṅgas. Consort: Pārvatī/Śakti. Sons: Gaṇeśa, Skanda. Vāhana: Nandi (bull). Abode: Kailāsa. Key texts: Śiva Purāṇa, Liṅga Purāṇa, Śaiva Āgamas, Tirumuṟai (Tamil). Festivals: Mahāśivarātri, Pradosha, Kārttikai Tīpam. --- A major deity with diverse textual, ritual, and regional forms; this record does not impose a single theology on the many traditions that center on Śiva.

title: Skanda
description: A deity with prominent roles in Purāṇic, Tamil, and regional traditions; his narratives and epithets vary significantly across textual and geographical contexts.

title: Sūrya
description: The solar deity represented in Vedic, Puranic, and living traditions; this record distinguishes textual portrayals from later syncretic developments.

title: Viṣṇu
description: Viṣṇu (विष्णु / விஷ்ணு / ವಿಷ್ಣು / വിഷ്ണു / বিষ্ণુ / વિષ્ણು), the All-Pervading One, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Vāsudeva, Govinda, Madhava, Keśava. Central to Vaiṣṇava traditions (Śrīvaiṣṇavism, Gauḍīya, Puṣṭimārga, Nimbārka, Madhva). Ten principal avatāras (daśāvatāra): Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki. Consort: Lakṣmī/Śrī. Abode: Vaikuṇṭha. Vāhana: Garuḍa. Attributes: Śaṅkha (conch), Cakra (discus), Gada (mace), Padma (lotus). Key texts: Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Nārāyaṇīya, Pāñcarātra Āgamas, Nālāyira Divya Prabandham (Tamil). Festivals: Janmāṣṭamī, Rāma-navamī, Vaikuṇṭha Ekādaśī, Onam (Vāmana), Dīpāvalī. --- A major deity with diverse textual, ritual, and regional forms; this record does not impose a single theology on the many traditions that center on Viṣṇu.

title: Viṭṭhala
description: Viṭṭhala (Vithoba, Paṇḍurāṅga), the deity of Pandharpur, Maharashtra, a form of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa standing on a brick (viṭ); the Vārkarī tradition, the annual Palkhi pilgrimage from Alandi and Dehu, the abhangas of Jñāneśvar and Tukārām; his dark complexion, hands on hips posture, and the Chandrabhaga river are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Adhika Māsa
description: The intercalary lunar month inserted approximately every 32.5 months to align lunar and solar calendars; considered especially auspicious for ritual and charity.

title: Akṣaya Tṛtīyā
description: A festival falling on the third lunar day of bright Vaiśākha, associated with prosperity, new ventures, and the descent of Gaṅgā; observances vary by region and tradition.

title: Bihu
description: The Assamese festival cycle of three Bihus (Rongali, Kongali, Bhogali) aligned with agricultural seasons; Rongali Bihu in April is the most prominent.

title: Cāturmāsya
description: The four-month monsoon period (Āṣāḍha–Kārttika) when ascetics traditionally remain stationary and householders observe additional vows; its observances vary by tradition.

title: Chhath Pūjā
description: A festival dedicated to Sūrya and Chhathī Maiyā, observed primarily in Bihar, Jharkhand, and eastern Uttar Pradesh with rigorous fasting, river bathing, and sunrise/sunset offerings.

title: Deva Uthānī Ekādaśī
description: The Ekādaśī in bright Kārttika marking Viṣṇu's awakening from cosmic sleep (yoganidrā); marks the end of Cāturmāsya and resumption of auspicious activities.

title: Dīpāvalī
description: Dīpāvalī (दीपावली / தீபாவளி / ദീപാവലি / दिवाळी), the Festival of Lights (dīpa-āvalī = row of lamps). Five days: Dhanteras (wealth, Dhanvantarī), Narka Caturdashī (Kṛṣṇa slays Narakāsura), Amāvasyā (main day, Lakṣmī Pūjā, Rāma's return to Ayodhyā), Govardhan Pūjā (Kṛṣṇa lifts Govardhan), Bhāi Dooj (sibling bond). Lighting dīpas (oil lamps), rangoli, fireworks, sweets, new clothes. Regional: Kālī Pūjā (Bengal, same night), Bandi Chhor Divas (Sikh, Guru Hargobind's release), Bestu Varas (Gujarati New Year), Balipratipada (Maharashtra). Jain: Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa. The universal celebration of light over darkness, knowledge over ignorance. --- A festival of lights observed across regions and communities with varied narratives, rituals, and historical associations.

title: Vijayadaśamī / Dussehra
description: Vijayadaśamī (Dussehra), the tenth day after Navarātri, celebrating the victory of good over evil: Durgā's victory over Mahiṣāsura (East/West India) and Rāma's victory over Rāvaṇa (North India); observed with Rāmalīlā enactments, effigy burning (Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Meghanāda), and the worship of weapons (śastra-pūjā); its regional variations are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gaṇeśa Caturthī
description: Gaṇeśa Caturthī, the ten-day festival celebrating Gaṇeśa's birth, observed in Bhādrapada (Aug–Sep); clay idol installation, daily pūjā, modak offerings, and immersion (visarjan) on Ananta Caturdaśī; its community celebrations (Sarvajanik Gaṇeśotsav) in Maharashtra, Goa, and Karnataka are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Gītā Jayantī
description: A festival commemorating the Bhagavad Gītā's revelation, observed on Mokṣadā Ekādaśī in Mārgaśīrṣa; its observances include recitation and discourse.

title: Guru Pūrṇimā
description: A festival honoring spiritual teachers, observed on the full moon of Āṣāḍha in Hindu traditions; Buddhist and Jain traditions observe related festivals on different dates; specific observances vary by lineage and region.

title: Hartālika Tīja
description: A festival observed primarily by women in North and Central India for marital well-being, associated with Pārvatī's penance for Śiva; practices vary by region.

title: Holī
description: Holī, the spring festival of colours observed on the full moon of Phālguna (Feb–Mar); the evening Holikā Dahan (bonfire) commemorating Prahlāda's survival, and the day of colour play (Raṅgavalī Holī) celebrating divine love (Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa); regional variations include Lathmār Holī (Barsana) and Hola Mohalla (Sikh, Punjab) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī
description: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī, the festival of Kṛṣṇa's birth, observed on the eighth day (aṣṭamī) of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada (Aug–Sep); midnight celebration of Kṛṣṇa's birth, fasting, bhajans, dahi handi (pot-breaking) in Maharashtra, Rāsa Līlā enactments in Vṛndāvana; its regional variations are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kārttikai Deepam
description: The Tamil festival of lights on the full moon of Kārttikai (Nov–Dec), dedicated to Śiva as the infinite light; its observance with rows of oil lamps (agal vilakku) and the Arunachalesvara temple beacon are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Kumbha Melā
description: A massive periodic pilgrimage festival held at four sites—Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, and Nashik—on different cycles; its historical development, sectarian participation, and site-specific management are complex and varied.

title: Lohrī
description: A Punjabi winter festival marking the passing of the winter solstice, celebrated with bonfires, folk songs, and distribution of sweets; its observances are regionally specific.

title: Māgha Mela
description: The annual Māgha Mela at Prayāgraja (Allahabad), Uttar Pradesh, during the month of Māgha (Jan–Feb), a smaller precursor to the Kumbha Mela; its ritual bathing, kalpavās, and regional significance are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---

title: Mahāśivarātri
